rv.q: Lloyd’s production, which premiered in August at the National Theater in London, poses the play’s philosophical inquiries on a stark and minimal plane that feels both cosmic and atomically intimate.
The play has had an indelible effect on me, and its big questions about mentality versus reality are lodged in my brain.
The changes work, and attest to the universal emotions and ethical dilemmas of the play...

Vocally and physically, it’s a well-balanced quartet: Russell the inscrutable, breathy waif, Essiedu with a dancer’s grace and rascally charm, Austin rueful and sympathetic, and Holdbrook-Smith wielding a velvety basso.
"The Effect" is not a great play, but it delivers and it also cheats.
But it’s a conceptual imposition, which paradoxically keeps intellectual engagement secondary, at best.
While the central courtship is at times charmingly depicted, the writing proves so schematic and artificial that the play not only takes place in a lab but feels like it was written in one as well.

Lloyd’s contrivances are so top-down overstimulating that the volunteers’ connection feels beside the point, leaving Taylor Russell and Paapa Essiedu’s alluring lead characterizations — ostensibly the play’s raison d'etre — entirely secondary.
The Effect has given us a huge gymnasium into which we are invited to play, engage, risk, contemplate, judge, experiment, and be our wild selves.
Director Jamie Lloyd's production, first mounted last year in London, sizzles with sensational performances by an unlikely couple...

cn.t: Critics are split on this revival of Lucy Prebble's brainy drama about love and brain chemistry. Performances earn wide praise, but Lloyd's stark staging divides—some find it riveting, others cold and clinical.

vr.q: The performances really hooked me and sustained my captivation the entire time
